title: Sense pleasures (Sn 4.1)
hookLine: read the first poem: desire fulfilled and desire thwarted
tomorrow: the next poem finds someone stuck in a cave. which cave?

cards: The tracking page said out for delivery all afternoon. You refreshed it again and again. Now the box is on the step, and for a little while it's wonderful.
Or the other ending: delivery failed, and it ruins the whole evening. Same wanting, two endings. An old poem describes both, and it gives the second one a very specific shape: an arrow.

teach.b: The poem opens the Atthakavagga, the chapter of eights, inside the Sutta Nipata, a collection of the Buddha's teachings in verse. It's short enough to read in a minute, so here it is, in plain paraphrase.

teach.h: GOT IT: GLAD. LOST IT: AN ARROW.
teach.b: When someone who longs for sense pleasures gets them, they're glad at heart. They got what they wanted. But when those pleasures fail them, they're hurt as if an arrow had gone in.
Then an image you can feel in your foot.
Whoever steps around sense desires the way you step around a snake's head, watchfully, gets past the pull. Then a list: fields, land, gold, cattle, horses, people, family.
Grab at them greedily and small weaknesses take over, troubles crush you, and pain seeps in like water into a broken boat.
So, the poem ends, stay mindful, bail out the boat, and reach the far shore. Notice that the poem never calls the pleasure fake. The gladness is real.
The point is the grip: the harder something hooks you, the deeper the arrow if it's taken away. That's why the line for today is a question. Not stop wanting.
What do I want, and how hard does it hold me?

how: The chapter of eights (Atthakavagga) is the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata; Theravada monastics and lay students study and chant its poems, and some teachers read them one at a time with a group.

o: a sixth sense that knows what others want
what the five senses enjoy, and our grip on it
the pleasures a monk is allowed on feast days

games.q: the poem's pictures — tap the pairs.
p: what losing a craved pleasure feels like
where bailing out the boat leads

s: the poem says sense pleasures don't really feel good
it says plainly that getting them makes a person glad. the trouble is the grip.
in the poem, losing a craved pleasure is compared to an arrow
when the pleasures fail, the person is hurt as if pierced by an arrow.
the Atthakavagga is a chapter of the Sutta Nipata
it's the chapter of eights, and this poem opens it.

games.q: a limited sneaker release sells out before you can check out. you're furious for days. by the poem, where did the arrow come from?
o: the grip of the wanting, there before anything sold out.
the store's unfair system for selling the shoes.
liking nice things at all; the poem says want nothing.
games.why: the poem puts the arrow in the grip: the harder something hooks you, the deeper it goes when it's lost. it doesn't say the shoes, or the gladness, were fake.

practice: Pick up something you want right now: your phone, a snack, the next episode's remote. Hold it in your hand without using it.
Feel where the wanting lives in your body, the jaw, the chest, the fingers, and breathe with it until the bell, the way you'd watch a snake from a safe step away.

wordCard.voice: Sense pleasures: what the eyes, ears, nose, tongue and body enjoy. In this poem, the gladness of getting them is real, and so is the arrow of losing them.

orig.note: Pali: sense desire, sense pleasure. The poem's Pali name is the Kāma Sutta.

carryVoice: The line to keep: what do I want, asked before the box arrives. Poem one, read.
